title: Evidence for an effective gauge field in flakes of superconducting 4Hb-TaS2
authors: Shalev Gur, T. R. Devidas, Eylon Persky, Roni Anna Gofman, Irena Feldman, Avior Almoalem, Sudip Kumar Saha, Mark H. Fischer, Avraham Klein, Jonathan Ruhman, Amit Kanigel, Beena Kalisky
abstract: Understanding the normal state of unconventional superconductors is central to uncovering the origin of superconductivity itself. Unconventional superconductivity often emerges from correlated electronic states characterized by intertwined symmetry-breaking orders. A striking example is 4Hb-TaS2, whose superconducting state exhibits a remarkable range of phenomena, including an unusual magnetic memory effect. Previous experiments showed that magnetic memory can be encoded above Tc and later revealed through spontaneous vortices below Tc, suggesting time-reversal symmetry breaking. However, since memory and vorticity are intertwined, this prevents establishing whether the effect results from trapped flux, weak conventional magnetism, or a true hidden electronic order. Here, we show that magnetic memory persists in the vortex-free Meissner regime of exfoliated 4Hb-TaS2 flakes, where it appears as a stable remanent modification of the superconducting screening response. Our results rule out explanations based on trapped vortices. Furthermore, the spatial profile of the flux generated by trained samples at zero field is inconsistent with conventional weak magnetism, suggesting a hidden electronic phase that imprints an effective flux on the superconducting condensate.
summary: This work analyzes magnetic memory in superconducting 4Hb-TaS2 flakes, showing the memory persists even when vortices are absent. By comparing experimental flux profiles to theoretical models, the authors argue that the memory is not due to trapped flux or simple magnetism, but rather points toward a hidden electronic phase coupling to the superconducting condensate via an effective gauge field.
main_problem: The paper investigates the origin of magnetic memory effects observed in unconventional superconductors, specifically determining if this memory arises from trapped magnetic flux, weak conventional magnetism, or a novel hidden electronic order.
main_result: The observed magnetic memory persists in the vortex-free Meissner regime and exhibits a spatial profile consistent with an effective, non-magnetic flux imprinted on the superconducting condensate, suggesting a hidden electronic phase.
method: The study combines advanced experimental magnetometry (SQUID measurements on exfoliated flakes) with theoretical modeling based on the Ginzburg-Landau free energy functional.
model_or_system: The system is superconducting flakes of 4Hb-TaS2, modeled using the Ginzburg-Landau theory which incorporates superconducting order parameters and magnetic coupling terms. The analysis distinguishes between screening currents from external fields and currents generated by internal magnetization.
key_observables: Magnetic memory signal ($\Delta\Phi_{	ext{rem}}$), spatial flux profiles, and the ratio $\Delta\Phi_{	ext{rem}}/\Delta\Phi_{	ext{ZFC}}$ (found to be $\approx 0.11 - 0.12$).
important_parameters: Superconducting transition temperature ($T_c$), penetration depth ($\lambda$), coherence length ($\xi$), and the ratio $\kappa = \lambda/\xi$.
main_assumptions: The analysis rules out explanations based on trapped vortices or ordinary weak magnetism, focusing on the memory's proportionality to the screening response.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the ZFC/FC protocols showing remanent flux maps, and supplementary figures validate the spatial uniformity and waiting-time independence of this memory signal.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from initial experimental observations of memory in the Meissner regime, ruling out vortex-trapping mechanisms, to detailed theoretical modeling using GL theory to distinguish between internal magnetization sources and effective gauge field coupling.
why_interesting: The concept of an 'effective gauge field' coupling to the superconducting condensate is highly relevant to understanding exotic pairing mechanisms and emergent gauge symmetries in strongly correlated superconductors.
